blocks.x: If you’ve registered for the JLPT and hit the point where self-study isn’t cutting it anymore, you’ve probably already started searching for a JLPT prep course. And that search gets harder fast if you’re taking the exam outside Japan or hoping to study online.

While there are plenty of online Japanese lessons out there, there are surprisingly few actual JLPT-focused courses. Even when you find one, there’s still the matter of finding a class with the right schedule: navigating time zones and pricing structures that aren’t always clear upfront.
So we did the legwork. Below are the best JLPT online courses available right now, with pricing, pros, cons, and what to weigh before you commit.
How Are JLPT Courses Different from Regular Japanese Courses?
So what’s the difference between a JLPT course and a regular Japanese course?
The short answer: a regular Japanese course teaches you to use the language; a JLPT course teaches you to pass a specific test. They overlap, but their priorities are different.

Regular courses (like Coto Academy’s typical Japanese lessons) are built around speaking and practical use. You’re learning to hold a conversation, order food, get through a job interview, and get that transfer to daily life in Japan. They don’t map cleanly onto how the JLPT actually tests you.

JLPT courses are built around one goal: passing the JLPT. On the content side, JLPT courses lean into grammar and analytical reading, which most conversation-based courses skip entirely, since it has little to do with speaking ability but a lot to do with passing.

On the practice side, expect regular mock tests under timed conditions rather than casual exercises, so you get used to the actual pacing before test day. And layered around all of that are exam-specific tips. Since it is usually taught by JLPT instructors, you will get tips like how to eliminate wrong answers fast, how to budget your time per section, and how question types tend to repeat across past exams.

The one-year course focuses on grammar and reading, and you can join anytime. It’s built for steady, ongoing progress and includes interactive exercises throughout, which makes it useful even if you’re not specifically preparing for the JLPT.

It’s not a live online JLPT course, but that’s kind of the point. If you’ve ever sat down to study JLPT by yourself and had no idea where to start or what to focus on next, J-Standard takes that guesswork off your plate. It walks you step by step through every unit and level, so instead of piecing together your own study plan from scratch, you just follow the path. It covers everything from hiragana and katakana through N5 to N2 grammar and vocabulary, all in one platform, all at your own pace.

The learning journey follows four steps. You start by watching teacher-led videos to learn new grammar and vocabulary, then apply it through real, practical dialogues based on everyday situations in Japan.
From there, you move into JLPT-style drills and quizzes to lock in what you’ve learned, and track it all on a simple dashboard that keeps your study hours and progress visible.

Currently, the platform has over 1,200 lessons and quizzes covering grammar, vocabulary, listening, and reading. We recommend it if you want something affordable and flexible enough to fit into a busy schedule, without sacrificing structure.

Best for: Learners who want fully personalized 1-on-1 tutoring and don’t mind doing some legwork to find the right tutor.
Available levelFlexible
DurationFlexible
Price$20 – 70/hour, depending on tutor
HighlightsPersonalized plan since it is typically 1-on-1 tutoring, but not always with professional instructors

You’ve probably already heard of Preply, a language platform that connects you with independent tutors. You can find tutors who specialize in JLPT prep and build a lesson plan around your specific goals.

The trade-off is consistency. Most tutors are native speakers, but not all of them are trained instructors, so teaching quality and JLPT-specific expertise can vary a lot from one tutor to the next. If you go this route, we recommend reading reviews and trying a few tutors before committing, since the experience depends on who you end up with.

Pricing varies and isn’t always affordable. Preply’s community tutors, meaning native speakers without formal certification, typically run $20 to $40 an hour. However, certified instructors cost more, usually $40 to $70 an hour, which adds up fast for private, one-on-one sessions.

The great thing is that because Preply usually only does 1-on-1 tutoring, it can work well if you want maximum flexibility and don’t mind doing some legwork to find the right fit, but it’s a less structured option compared to a dedicated JLPT platform like Coto Academy or J-Standard.

SNG’s Online JLPT Preparation Course covers all test sections: vocabulary, kanji, grammar, reading comprehension, and listening. Lessons use digital content to track your understanding as you go, and instructors focus extra time on whatever you’re struggling with most. You’ll get 30 hours of class time across 10 lessons, wrapping up with a final practice exam to confirm you’re ready for test day.

By the end of the course, you’ll have mastered the vocabulary, grammar, and kanji needed to pass the JLPT, built the listening skills to comprehend short conversations, and picked up test-taking strategies and tips to boost your overall score.

Kudan Institute takes a narrower approach than most JLPT courses on this list: it covers grammar only. Rather than splitting attention across vocabulary, reading, and listening, the course drills grammar patterns intensively over a six-week run, timed right before the JLPT exam.

The structure centers on pattern recognition. Grammar questions are broken down and sorted into recognizable question types, so instead of memorizing textbook entries in isolation, you learn to spot what a question is actually testing. Each session pairs that analysis with strategy review, and then interactive practice with the target grammar so it doesn’t stay theoretical.
Enrollment is open mid-course, so joining in week three is a genuine option if you’ve only just realized grammar is your weak point.

The catch is that lessons run in the evening Japan time on weekdays. If you’re in Europe or the Americas, evening JST lands in your morning on a workday: early morning for much of Europe and the middle of the night for parts of North America.

FAQ
What is the best JLPT online course?

It depends on what you need. Coto Academy is the strongest all-around pick if you want live instruction, professional JLPT instructors, and flexible scheduling. J-Standard is best if you want a self-paced, affordable option without live classes. Preply suits learners who want 1-on-1 tutoring and are willing to vet tutors themselves. There’s no single “best” course for everyone — the right one depends on your level, budget, time zone, and whether you want live or self-paced instruction.
Are JLPT online courses actually effective?

Yes, as long as the course is built around the exam rather than general conversation. A good JLPT course gives you timed mock tests, exam-specific strategy, and focused practice on the sections the real test weights heavily, like grammar and reading — things self-study and conversation-based classes typically don’t cover in depth.
How long does it take to prepare for the JLPT with an online course?

It varies by level and course. Short intensives like Kudan Institute or SNG run 2–3 months and are designed as a final push before the exam. Longer programs like Coto Academy’s one-year track suit learners building proficiency from the ground up. As a rule, the higher the level (N2, N1), the more prep time you should budget.
How much do JLPT online courses cost?

Pricing ranges widely: J-Standard starts around $69 for 3 months, Japonin runs from about ¥1,280 per lesson, and structured short-term intensives like SNG or Kudan run roughly ¥39,600–¥49,500 for a 2–3 month course. Live 1-on-1 tutoring through Preply is the most expensive per hour ($20–$70), since you’re paying for individual attention.
Do I need to already know Japanese to join a JLPT online course?

Most courses assume some prior study. J-Standard is the exception, starting from hiragana and katakana for true beginners. Others, like SNG, require a minimum number of self-study hours (300+ for N3, 600+ for N2) before enrolling.
